label: Appearance
value: The Woggle-Bug dresses in a dark-blue swallowtail coat.
unit: The Woggle-Bug is a great, round, buglike creature fully as tall as the Tin Woodman, standing upright on two slender legs ending in feet with curling toes. His flat body is a glistening dark brown on the back and striped with bands of light brown and white across the front, supported by a long neck and a head with bulging black eyes, a nose ending in a curling antenna, and ears bearing antennae like miniature pigtails. He dresses in a dark-blue swallowtail coat with yellow silk lining and a flower in the buttonhole, a tight white duck vest, fawn-colored plush knickerbockers with gilt knee buckles, and a tall silk hat set jauntily on his head.

What he saw was a great, round, buglike body supported upon two slender legs which ended in delicate feet—the toes curling upward. The body of the Woggle-Bug was rather flat, and judging from what could be seen of it was of a glistening dark brown color upon the back, while the front was striped with alternate bands of light brown and white, blending together at the edges. Its arms were fully as slender as its legs, and upon a rather long neck was perched its head—not unlike the head of a man, except that its nose ended in a curling antenna, or “feeler,” and its ears from the upper points bore antennae that decorated the sides of its head like two miniature, curling pig tails. It must be admitted that the round, black eyes were rather bulging in appearance; but the expression upon the Woggle-Bug’s face was by no means unpleasant.

Upon meeting Dorothy Gale, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman, he admitted his fearfulness and decided to join their expedition to the Emerald City to request courage from the Great Oz. Along the road of yellow brick, he served as a faithful companion and guardian, though he was temporarily overcome by a poisonous poppy field until saved by the Queen of the Field Mice and her subjects. Upon reaching the Emerald City, he received a potion from Oz which he swallowed, believing it gave him genuine courage. Afterwards, he continued to accompany Dorothy and his friends on their subsequent trials.

label: History
value: The Scarecrow mistakenly thought Jack was laughing at him.
unit: The Scarecrow sought out the Wizard of Oz to receive a brain. During his audience in the Throne Room, the Wizard unfastened his head, emptied the straw, and filled it with a mixture of bran, pins, and needles before restuffing it, leaving the Scarecrow feeling exceptionally wise. Later, while traveling with companions toward the Quadling country, he attempted to lead the group up a rocky hill guarded by the Hammer-Heads. Upon marching forward, he was struck by a shooting flat-topped head and sent tumbling down the hill, prompting Dorothy to call the Winged Monkeys for transport. After ascending the throne as King of the Emerald City, he met Jack Pumpkinhead and mistakenly thought Jack was laughing at him until realizing Jack's carved smile was permanent. Recognizing they spoke different regional tongues, he ordered an interpreter to be brought. During later journeys riding the Saw-Horse with Tip and Jack, his straw body became soaked, but Tip dried and restuffed him back into shape. As they traveled past familiar locations, the Scarecrow reminisced about past adventures, including saving Dorothy from stinging bees and being captured by Winged Monkeys.

label: History
value: He projected terrifying illusions such as a lovely Lady when granting audiences.
unit: Originally a balloonist and ventriloquist from Omaha, he accidentally arrived in the Land of Oz when his hot-air balloon drifted out of the clouds. Believing him to be a powerful wizard, the inhabitants accepted him as their ruler. He ordered the construction of the Emerald City and mandated that all residents and visitors wear locked green spectacles. In secret, he visited the witch Mombi to learn magic tricks and entrusted her with baby Princess Ozma. To preserve his reputation, he hid behind a screen in his throne room and projected terrifying illusions—such as a giant Head, a lovely Lady, a Beast, and a Ball of Fire—when granting audiences. When Dorothy Gale and her companions arrived seeking his aid, he demanded the destruction of the Wicked Witch of the West as payment. After Dorothy defeated the Witch and exposed him as a fraud, he ingeniously fulfilled his visitors' requests through clever tricks, giving brains to the Scarecrow, a heart to the Tin Woodman, and courage to the Cowardly Lion. He then constructed a hot-air balloon to return to Kansas with Dorothy, but the ropes snapped prematurely, carrying him away alone. Before drifting out of sight into the sky, he officially appointed the Scarecrow to succeed him as ruler of the Emerald City.

unit: Mombi lived in the northern Country of the Gillikins in the Land of Oz, where she was suspected of practicing magical arts. She acted as guardian to the young boy Tip, whom she made perform various household and field tasks while keeping him under her strict care. Long ago, the Wizard of Oz paid her three visits to entrust her with the baby Princess Ozma; Mombi hid the child by magically transforming her into Tip in exchange for learning the Wizard's magic tricks. Years later, when General Jinjur usurped the throne of the Emerald City, Mombi aided Jinjur and attempted to thwart Glinda the Sorceress through trickery. She used a spell to swap appearances with Jellia Jamb and later transformed herself into a red rose in the palace garden to evade capture. However, Glinda saw through her illusions and forced Jinjur to hand her over. Confronted by Glinda with a lie-detecting pearl and threatened with death, Mombi confessed that she had transformed Princess Ozma into Tip.

passages.v02:c03:p0000: In the Country of the Gillikins, which is at the North of the Land of Oz, lived a youth called Tip. There was more to his name than that, for old Mombi often declared that his whole name was Tippetarius; but no one was expected to say such a long word when “Tip” would do just as well.
passages.v02:c03:p0001: This boy remembered nothing of his parents, for he had been brought when quite young to be reared by the old woman known as Mombi, whose reputation, I am sorry to say, was none of the best. For the Gillikin people had reason to suspect her of indulging in magical arts, and therefore hesitated to associate with her.
passages.v02:c03:p0003: Tip was made to carry wood from the forest, that the old woman might boil her pot. He also worked in the corn-fields, hoeing and husking; and he fed the pigs and milked the four-horned cow that was Mombi’s especial pride.
passages.v02:c23:p0020: So Mombi called Jellia Jamb to her, and performed a certain magical rite with which she was familiar. As a result of the enchantment Jellia took on the form and features of Mombi, while the old witch grew to resemble the girl so closely that it seemed impossible anyone could guess the deception.
passages.v02:c23:p0028: This Jellia dared not tell, having been threatened with death by the witch if she confessed the fraud. But Glinda, sweet and fair though she was, understood magic better than any other person in the Land of Oz. So, by uttering a few potent words and making a peculiar gesture, she quickly transformed the girl into her proper shape, while at the same time old Mombi, far away in Jinjur’s palace, suddenly resumed her own crooked form and evil features.
passages.v02:c23:p0031: Then Jellia was forced to tell of the trick Mombi had played and she also begged Glinda’s protection, which the Sorceress readily granted. But Glinda was now really angry, and sent word to Jinjur that the fraud was discovered and she must deliver up the real Mombi or suffer terrible consequences. Jinjur was prepared for this message, for the witch well understood, when her natural form was thrust upon her, that Glinda had discovered her trickery. But the wicked old creature had already thought up a new deception, and had made Jinjur promise to carry it out. So the Queen said to Glinda’s messenger:

label: Personality
value: The Scarecrow takes comfort in the knowledge that damages to his body can easily be repaired.
unit: Despite his flimsy and awkward physical construction, the Scarecrow holds a reputation as the wisest personage in the Land of Oz. He is thoughtful, polite, and displays deep consideration and kindness for his companions. He exhibits a bright, cheerful demeanor even in difficult situations, taking comfort in the knowledge that damages to his body can easily be repaired.

passages.v02:c09:p0001: His Majesty the Scarecrow was dressed in a suit of faded blue clothes, and his head was merely a small sack stuffed with straw, upon which eyes, ears, a nose and a mouth had been rudely painted to represent a face. The clothes were also stuffed with straw, and that so unevenly or carelessly that his Majesty’s legs and arms seemed more bumpy than was necessary. Upon his hands were gloves with long fingers, and these were padded with cotton. Wisps of straw stuck out from the monarch’s coat and also from his neck and boot-tops. Upon his head he wore a heavy golden crown set thick with sparkling jewels, and the weight of this crown caused his brow to sag in wrinkles, giving a thoughtful expression to the painted face. Indeed, the crown alone betokened majesty; in all else the, Scarecrow King was but a simple scarecrow—flimsy, awkward, and unsubstantial.
passages.v02:c09:p0003: At first, indeed, His Majesty thought his queer visitor was laughing at him, and was inclined to resent such a liberty; but it was not without reason that the Scarecrow had attained the reputation of being the wisest personage in the Land of Oz. He made a more careful examination of his visitor, and soon discovered that Jack’s features were carved into a smile and that he could not look grave if he wished to.
passages.v02:c09:p0019: “Did you understand that sign?” asked His Majesty, politely.
passages.v02:c12:p0025: “Thank you very much,” said the monarch, brightly, as he walked about and found himself to be well balanced. “There are several distinct advantages in being a Scarecrow. For if one has friends near at hand to repair damages, nothing very serious can happen to you.”
passages.v02:c12:p0051: “Still, we must have consideration for this poor boy, who is made of flesh and blood and bone, and gets tired,” suggested the Scarecrow, in his usual thoughtful manner. “I remember it was the same way with little Dorothy. We always had to sit through the night while she slept.”

screen.reason: The passage explicitly states that the Scarecrow finds advantages in being a scarecrow because friends can repair damages to him.

label: History
value: The Tin Woodman aimed to restore the Scarecrow to his throne
unit: After the Wicked Witch of the West was destroyed, Dorothy and the Cowardly Lion set out with the yellow Winkies to find the Tin Woodman. They discovered him lying battered and bent on a rocky plain, whereupon Winkie tinsmiths hammered, soldered, and repaired him back to his original form. Upon reunited with his friends, he used his newly fitted gold-handled axe to chop down a tall tree, retrieving the Scarecrow's clothes so their comrade could be re-stuffed. Following the completion of their quest, the Tin Woodman visited the Wizard of Oz in the Emerald City, who placed a heart inside his tin breast, which the Woodman marked with an engraved star. He eventually became the nickel-plated Emperor of the Winkies, ruling from his castle. When his close friend the Scarecrow arrived with Tip and Jack Pumpkinhead seeking refuge after being deposed by General Jinjur's rebels, the Tin Woodman welcomed them warmly and immediately pledged his support and forces to march on the Emerald City and restore the Scarecrow to his throne. During their subsequent perils, he gallantly fought off swarms of attacking Jackdaws using his spinning axe to protect his comrades.

passages.v01:c15:p0005: So they called the yellow Winkies and asked them if they would help to rescue their friends, and the Winkies said that they would be delighted to do all in their power for Dorothy, who had set them free from bondage. So she chose a number of the Winkies who looked as if they knew the most, and they all started away. They traveled that day and part of the next until they came to the rocky plain where the Tin Woodman lay, all battered and bent. His axe was near him, but the blade was rusted and the handle broken off short.
passages.v01:c15:p0010: The tinsmiths looked the Woodman over carefully and then answered that they thought they could mend him so he would be as good as ever. So they set to work in one of the big yellow rooms of the castle and worked for three days and four nights, hammering and twisting and bending and soldering and polishing and pounding at the legs and body and head of the Tin Woodman, until at last he was straightened out into his old form, and his joints worked as well as ever. To be sure, there were several patches on him, but the tinsmiths did a good job, and as the Woodman was not a vain man he did not mind the patches at all.
passages.v01:c15:p0015: It was a very tall tree, and the trunk was so smooth that no one could climb it; but the Woodman said at once, “I’ll chop it down, and then we can get the Scarecrow’s clothes.”
passages.v01:c15:p0017: As soon as he had spoken, the Tin Woodman began to chop, and in a short time the tree fell over with a crash, whereupon the Scarecrow’s clothes fell out of the branches and rolled off on the ground.
passages.v02:c13:p0025: “My dear old friend! My noble comrade!” cried the Tin Woodman, joyfully. “how delighted! I am to meet you once again.”
passages.v02:c13:p0038: Tip, during this conversation, was looking at the Woodman with undisguised amazement, and noticed that the celebrated Emperor of the Winkies was composed entirely of pieces of tin, neatly soldered and riveted together into the form of a man. He rattled and clanked a little, as he moved, but in the main he seemed to be most cleverly constructed, and his appearance was only marred by the thick coating of polishing-paste that covered him from head to foot.

label: History
value: The task given by the Wizard was to defeat the Wicked Witch of the West.
unit: Dorothy was raised on the Kansas prairies by her Aunt Em and Uncle Henry alongside her small black dog, Toto. A powerful cyclone struck her home, lifting the house into the air with Dorothy and Toto inside and carrying it to the Land of Oz. The house landed on and unintentionally killed the Wicked Witch of the East, granting Dorothy the magical Silver Shoes and a protective kiss from the Good Witch of the North. Seeking a way back to Kansas, Dorothy set off toward the Emerald City along the yellow brick road to consult the Great Oz. Along the journey, she befriended and rescued the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion, who joined her quest. Upon reaching the Emerald City, the Wizard tasked the companions with defeating the Wicked Witch of the West. While forced into servitude in the Witch's castle, Dorothy successfully melted the Wicked Witch with a bucket of water after her Silver Shoe was stolen. Returning to the Emerald City, she discovered the Wizard was a humbug unable to grant her request magically. Eventually, Dorothy traveled south to Glinda the Good Witch, who revealed the secret power of her Silver Shoes, allowing Dorothy to safely tap her heels and return home to Kansas with Toto.

passages.v01:c03:p0000: Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer’s wife. Their house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room; and this room contained a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner. There was no garret at all, and no cellar—except a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose, mighty enough to crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.
passages.v01:c03:p0011: Toto jumped out of Dorothy’s arms and hid under the bed, and the girl started to get him. Aunt Em, badly frightened, threw open the trap door in the floor and climbed down the ladder into the small, dark hole. Dorothy caught Toto at last and started to follow her aunt. When she was halfway across the room there came a great shriek from the wind, and the house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly upon the floor.
passages.v01:c03:p0014: The north and south winds met where the house stood, and made it the exact center of the cyclone. In the middle of a cyclone the air is generally still, but the great pressure of the wind on every side of the house raised it up higher and higher, until it was at the very top of the cyclone; and there it remained and was carried miles and miles away as easily as you could carry a feather.
passages.v01:c14:p0059: Dorothy followed her through many of the beautiful rooms in her castle until they came to the kitchen, where the Witch bade her clean the pots and kettles and sweep the floor and keep the fire fed with wood.
passages.v01:c14:p0060: Dorothy went to work meekly, with her mind made up to work as hard as she could; for she was glad the Wicked Witch had decided not to kill her.
passages.v01:c14:p0067: Dorothy’s life became very sad as she grew to understand that it would be harder than ever to get back to Kansas and Aunt Em again. Sometimes she would cry bitterly for hours, with Toto sitting at her feet and looking into her face, whining dismally to show how sorry he was for his little mistress. Toto did not really care whether he was in Kansas or the Land of Oz so long as Dorothy was with him; but he knew the little girl was unhappy, and that made him unhappy too.
